design_detail: Retrospective population cohort from linked Taiwanese administrative databases, 2007–2016: the Taiwan Illicit Drug Issue Database (TIDID: drug-abuse prevention case records, police drug-crime and penalty data, Ministry of Justice deferred-prosecution data) linked by encrypted identifier to National Health Insurance claims (NHIRD). Exposed: 74,601 adults whose first arrest for illicit use of an amphetamine-type substance (every arrest with a positive urine test; the 23 listed substances include methamphetamine, amphetamine, MDMA and MDA) fell in the period; index date = first arrest. Comparison: 298,404 insured adults with no record of illicit drug use, four per exposed person, frequency matched on index year, age and sex, with a random index month and day. People with a recorded psychosis diagnosis before the index date were excluded from both groups. Outcome: first recorded psychosis diagnosis (ICD-9-CM claims), followed to diagnosis, death or 31 December 2016. Cox models adjusted for age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses; Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence; strata by age, sex, comorbidity, number of arrests and rehabilitation under deferred prosecution.
can_establish: That adults arrested for amphetamine-type substance use in Taiwan had a first psychosis diagnosis recorded more often in the following years than insured adults of the same age, sex and index year with no record of illicit drug use, and how large that difference was in rates per person-year and in cumulative incidence.
cannot_establish: That amphetamine use caused the psychosis (adjustment only for age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses, some recorded after the index date; no adjustment for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position, family history or other psychiatric history); a risk specific to methamphetamine (the substances are not broken down); a dose–response (the number of arrests is counted over the whole follow-up and reflects police contact); or that rehabilitation under deferred prosecution lowers risk (prosecutors offered it to about 10% judged to have promising treatment outcomes).

sample.recruitment: Registry. TIDID holds date of birth, sex, arrest records and deferred prosecution for rehabilitation treatment; National Health Insurance is a compulsory single-payer programme covering 99% of the population, and its claims form the NHIRD (Methods › Data source, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Comparison people were drawn from beneficiaries with no record of illicit drug use who were insured in the index year of the exposed person they were matched to (Methods › Study population, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults aged 18 or older resident in Taiwan, followed from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2016. Exposed: arrested for illicit use of one of 23 listed amphetamine-type substances (amphetamine, dexamphetamine, levamphetamine, methamphetamine and its racemate, levomethamphetamine, MDMA, MDA, MDEA, N-hydroxy-MDA, brolamfetamine, DOM, DOET, 2,5-dimethoxyamphetamine, 4-methoxyamphetamine, TMA, 5-methoxy-MDA, N-ethylamphetamine, N,N-dimethylamphetamine, fluoro-, chloro- and methoxymethamphetamine, lisdexamphetamine), every arrest accompanied by a positive urine test; index date = first arrest. Both groups: excluded if a psychosis diagnosis (ICD-9-CM 291.3, 291.5, 292.1, 292.11, 292.12, 293.81, 293.82, 295, 296.04–296.64 with psychotic features, 297, 297.3, 298.0, 298.1, 298.4, 298.8, 298.9, 780.1) was recorded before the index date (Methods › Study population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The look-back period for earlier diagnoses, whether arrests before 2007 were considered in choosing the first arrest, and the counts excluded at each step (given only in the Figure 1 flowchart, an image) are not stated in the text.
sample.demographics: Mean age 33.3 (SD 9.45) in both cohorts; 84.2% men; aged 18–29 38.2%, 30–44 49.1%, 45 or older 12.7% (identical by design). Comorbidities, amphetamine vs non-amphetamine cohort: depression 1.98% vs 0.42% (SMD 0.14), anxiety 0.91% vs 0.27% (0.08), ischaemic heart disease 1.32% vs 0.78% (0.05), cardiovascular disease 0.79% vs 0.45% (0.04), stroke 1.31% vs 0.66% (0.07) (Findings, 1st paragraph; Table 1). No data on education, income, occupation, ethnic group, alcohol or other drug use, or psychiatric history beyond these codes.
sample.attrition: Followed from the index date to a psychosis diagnosis, death or 31 December 2016: mean 4.93 (SD 2.93) years in the amphetamine cohort and 4.99 (2.93) in the comparison cohort; 367,696 and 1,487,536 person-years (Findings, 1st paragraph; Table 2). Deaths are treated as censoring and their number is not reported; loss of insurance cover, emigration and time in prison are not discussed.
sample.selection_effects: The exposed group is defined by arrest, not by use. The authors note that arrests reflect police activity and priorities, that many people who use amphetamines are never arrested (so the comparison group may include some), and that people who use more often may be more likely to be arrested (Conclusions and clinical implications, 6th paragraph). The comparison group excludes anyone with any record of illicit drug use, so it is the general insured population, not people who use other drugs; differences in other drug use, alcohol and socio-economic position are built into the comparison. The rehabilitation subgroup was chosen by prosecutors, who offered deferred prosecution to about 10% judged to have promising treatment outcomes (8th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Administrative record of arrest for illicit amphetamine-type substance use, each arrest accompanied by a positive urine test (Methods › Study population, 1st paragraph). Exposure is fixed at the first arrest; later use is unknown. The number of arrests is counted from the index date to the end of the study, and the authors treat it as implying cumulative dose (Methods › Statistics, 1st paragraph). Rehabilitation treatment comes from the deferred-prosecution records (Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: the authors state that the database has no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity of dependence (Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph) and that periods and doses of use could not be obtained (10th paragraph). Number of arrests: one 40,880 people, two 15,026, three 7,710, four 4,413, five or more 6,572 (Table 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not adjusted for. Other drug use by the exposed group is recorded in the same database (the comparison group is defined by having no such record) but is neither reported nor used for adjustment; alcohol use is not reported. The substances counted as amphetamine include MDMA, MDA and other ring-substituted amphetamines, and no breakdown by substance (for example the share involving methamphetamine) is given.

comparison.controls: 298,404 insured adults with no record of illicit drug use, four per exposed person, randomly selected after frequency matching on index year, age and sex; index month and day assigned at random within the index year; those with an earlier psychosis diagnosis excluded (Methods › Study population, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Frequency matched on index year, age and sex (identical distributions, Table 1). Not matched or adjusted on socio-economic status: the authors note that people who use amphetamines often have lower socio-economic status but argue, citing controversy about socio-economic status and psychosis, that omitting it might not have affected the results (Conclusions and clinical implications, 7th paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genetic data, ethnic group, obstetric complications and childhood adversity (named by the authors as unavailable, 8th paragraph); also, not mentioned by the authors, family history of psychosis, education and psychiatric history other than the five comorbidity codes; socio-economic position was not matched (7th paragraph). Other drug use is recorded in the same database (the comparison group is defined by having no such record) but is not used for adjustment.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: None recorded by design (no record of illicit drug use); alcohol and tobacco use unknown; the authors note that some may have used amphetamines without being arrested.

outcomes.instruments: Diagnoses in National Health Insurance claims, ICD-9-CM. Outcome codes listed: 295, 296.04, 296.14, 296.24, 296.34, 296.44, 296.54, 296.64, 297, 298.0, 298.1, 298.4, 298.8, 298.9 and 780.1, following Moran et al. (2019) (Methods › Study population, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of the codes in this population is reported. The authors note that rehabilitation under deferred prosecution took place in hospital psychiatric departments, which might increase the chance of a diagnosis (Conclusions and clinical implications, 8th paragraph). The comparison group's rate (0.77 per 1,000 person-years, 77 per 100,000) is 2.4 to 2.9 times the pooled incidence of psychotic disorders the authors cite (31.7 and 26.6 per 100,000 person-years) and lies between two US rates of first psychotic symptoms (46 and 86 per 100,000) (2nd paragraph; editors' arithmetic), consistent with a broad code set that includes hallucinations and affective disorders with psychotic features.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis = a first recorded claim with one of the listed outcome codes. The text says the definition includes other stimulant use disorders with psychosis, but the outcome code list omits the drug-induced psychosis codes (292.1, 292.11, 292.12) that are in the exclusion list (see reporting issues). How many claims, or what kind of visit, were required is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 14 adjusted hazard ratios (overall; three age, two sex and two comorbidity strata; five arrest categories; rehabilitation) and one trend test, each at two-sided p<0.05 (Methods › Statistics, 2nd paragraph). The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and that the results should be considered exploratory (Methods › Data source, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (routinely recorded diagnoses); clinicians who recorded diagnoses may have known about drug use or arrest.

analysis.effect_sizes: First recorded psychosis: 1,722 events in 367,696 person-years (4.68 per 1,000) in the amphetamine cohort against 1,144 in 1,487,536 (0.77 per 1,000); crude HR 6.08 (95% CI 5.64–6.55); HR 5.28 (4.90–5.70) adjusted for age, sex and comorbidities (Table 2). Rate difference about 3.9 per 1,000 person-years (editors' calculation). Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence at 10 years 3.75% against 0.63%, log-rank p<0.0001 (Findings, 2nd paragraph). Adjusted HRs by stratum: ages 18–29 5.09 (4.50–5.75), 30–44 5.33 (4.79–5.93), 45 or older 5.41 (4.29–6.82); men 4.81 (4.42–5.24), women 7.49 (6.30–8.91), from rates of 4.16 and 7.33 against 0.77 and 0.78 per 1,000; without comorbidity 6.30 (5.79–6.86), with comorbidity 2.28 (1.93–2.69), from rates of 3.91 against 0.62 and 20.02 against 7.39 per 1,000, so the rate difference is larger with comorbidity (about 12.6 against 3.3 per 1,000; editors' calculation). Number of arrests, adjusted: one 4.49 (4.09–4.93), two 5.07 (4.51–5.72), three 5.24 (4.52–6.09), four 5.53 (4.60–6.64), five or more 6.25 (5.42–7.20); p for trend 0.038 (Table 3). Rehabilitation against none, within the amphetamine cohort: 112 events in 29,884 person-years (3.75 per 1,000) against 1,610 in 337,812 (4.77); crude HR 0.74 (0.61–0.90), adjusted 0.74 (0.61–0.89) (Table 4).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex and five comorbidities (depression, anxiety, ischaemic heart disease, cardiovascular disease, stroke) diagnosed at any time during 2007–2016, not only before the index date (Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 footnote †); number of arrests added in the rehabilitation model (Table 4 footnote). No adjustment for socio-economic position, alcohol or other drug use, or psychiatric history.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and that the results should be considered exploratory (Methods › Data source, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: One overall model with many strata and no sensitivity analyses (no lag period after the arrest, no restriction to methamphetamine, no analysis of substance-induced against other psychoses); no test of proportional hazards (the authors say a single average HR may mislead, 9th paragraph of the Conclusions); no interaction tests for the sex and comorbidity differences; the trend test is not described; the breakdown of the exposed group by substance and the counts at each selection step are not given in the text.
analysis.power: Not an issue for the main estimate (1,722 and 1,144 events); the rehabilitation comparison rests on 112 events among 7,733 people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In linked administrative records, adults arrested for amphetamine-type substance use had a first psychosis diagnosis recorded at about six times the rate of insured adults of the same age, sex and index year with no drug record (4.68 against 0.77 per 1,000 person-years; 10-year cumulative incidence 3.75% against 0.63%), HR 5.28 after adjustment for age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses only. The HR was larger in women and rose from 4.49 with one arrest to 6.25 with five or more; within the arrested group, the roughly 10% chosen by prosecutors for rehabilitation had a lower rate (HR 0.74).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that people with illicit amphetamine use were "5.28 times more likely" to experience psychosis and reports a significant decrease in risk with rehabilitation; the discussion infers "a direct effect of amphetamine" from the larger HR in people without comorbidity (Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph) and "a preventive effect of psychotherapy" from the rehabilitation comparison (5th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the comparison group had no drug record, and other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position and family history were not adjusted for, while the adjustment used comorbidities recorded after the index date; (2) the smaller HR with comorbidity reflects a baseline rate about twelve times higher in that stratum: the rate difference is larger with comorbidity (12.6 against 3.3 per 1,000 person-years), so it does not point to a direct effect; (3) the rehabilitation group was chosen by prosecutors for promising outcomes, the timing of treatment relative to follow-up is not described, and the treatment's content is never described although the discussion calls it psychotherapy, so the lower HR cannot be read as an effect of treatment; (4) the arrest gradient uses arrests counted over the whole follow-up, which accumulate with time observed (about 4.4 person-years per person with one arrest against 6.5 with five or more; editors' calculation) and with police contact, so it is not a dose–response, as the authors themselves concede for dose; (5) amphetamine here includes MDMA and other substances without a breakdown; (6) the larger HR in women (7.49 against 4.81) is called a greater risk of amphetamine-induced psychosis and given a hormonal explanation from animal studies (4th paragraph), although no interaction test is reported and the same paragraph offers a confounding explanation (women arrested were more disadvantaged). The authors do state that the analysis was exploratory and not preregistered, that arrest is a proxy for use, that amphetamine might precipitate rather than cause psychotic symptoms in people already vulnerable, and that confounders such as childhood adversity could not be controlled (6th to 10th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Prospective within-person study of people with methamphetamine dependence showing dose-related psychotic symptoms, cited by the authors in support of their arrest gradient (their ref. 24)
Systematic review of risk factors for methamphetamine-associated psychosis, cited by the authors for amphetamine use as the primary risk factor (their ref. 23)
Moran et al. (2019), psychosis with methylphenidate or amphetamine in patients with ADHD, the source of the outcome definition (their ref. 19); not read
Meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies: amphetamine use disorder and psychosis, adjusted OR 2.4 (1.6–3.5; 4 studies)
This study: arrest-defined exposure in a national registry, HR 5.28 against people with no drug record
General-population birth cohort (New Zealand): any use in a period, OR 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment including concurrent cannabis use

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the association is found across designs, but its size depends on the comparison and the adjustment: about 2.4 for use disorder in the meta-analysis of mostly within-sample comparisons, 1.33 in a general-population birth cohort after adjustment including cannabis, and 5.28 here against people with no drug record and minimal adjustment. This is the largest cohort read so far and the only one giving rates of new recorded diagnoses after a dated index event, but it cannot separate methamphetamine from other amphetamine-type substances, or the drug from the other circumstances of people who are arrested.

funding.funder: Supported in part by the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST 104-3011-F-039-001), the Ministry of Health and Welfare (M05B4352), the National Health Research Institutes (NP-108-GP-05), the Ministry of Health and Welfare Clinical Trial Centre (MOHW109-TDU-B-212-114004), and China Medical University Hospital and China Medical University under the Higher Education Sprout Project of the Ministry of Education, Taiwan; the funders had no role in study design, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.affiliations_note: Tsaotun Psychiatric Centre (Ministry of Health and Welfare), China Medical University School of Medicine and Graduate Institute of Biomedical Sciences, and China Medical University Hospital (Management Office for Health Data; Centre for Drug Abuse and Addiction), Taiwan. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A linkage of the same registries that identifies methamphetamine specifically, starts follow-up after a lag from the first recorded use, compares people arrested for methamphetamine with people arrested for other drugs (or with siblings), adjusts for other substance use, alcohol, socio-economic position and psychiatric contact measured before the index date, treats arrests and treatment as time-varying, and reports substance-induced and primary psychotic disorders separately.

domains.note: Adjusted only for age and sex (matched) and five comorbidity diagnoses that were recorded at any time in 2007–2016, so partly after exposure, and whose depression codes include two outcome codes (296.24, 296.34). No adjustment for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position, family history or earlier psychiatric contact, all expected to be strongly related both to arrest for drug use and to psychosis, against a comparison group with no record of any illicit drug use. A second reader may judge this high rather than very high; the overall would then be high.

Arrest with a positive urine test is specific for some use at the time but insensitive (most use is never detected and the comparison group may include people who use); exposure is fixed at the first arrest; 23 substances including MDMA are pooled without a breakdown; the number of arrests is counted over the whole follow-up.

Exposure is defined by arrest, which selects people with police contact and possibly heavier or more visible use; follow-up starts at the first arrest, not at the start of use, so people whose psychosis was diagnosed before their first arrest are excluded while episodes that led to an arrest and were diagnosed afterwards count as new; the look-back for earlier diagnoses is not stated.

Arrest is followed by prosecution, deferred prosecution with hospital treatment for about 10%, and possibly imprisonment (not discussed); these change both later use and contact with services, and the rehabilitation comparison is itself an intervention allocated by prosecutors.
Registry linkage appears complete, but the counts excluded at each step are only in a flowchart image, deaths (censored) are not counted, and loss of insurance cover is not addressed.

Claims diagnoses not validated in this population; the listed outcome codes omit the drug-induced psychosis codes that the text says were included; people arrested for drug use, and particularly those treated in hospital psychiatric departments under deferred prosecution, are likely to have more contact with services where a diagnosis can be recorded (the authors note this for the rehabilitation group).

Not preregistered and described as exploratory; many strata, no sensitivity analyses, and an undescribed trend test whose printed p value is reproduced by a regression on five category rates (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The association is large and precisely estimated, and the design gives rates of new recorded diagnoses after a dated index event, which most of this literature lacks. But the comparison is between people arrested for drug use and insured people with no drug record, adjusted only for age, sex and five comorbidity codes partly recorded after exposure; other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position, family history, earlier psychiatric contact and greater contact with services after arrest could each account for a large part of an HR of 5.28, and every one of these biases would make the estimate larger. It may be cited for the rates of first recorded psychosis diagnoses after an amphetamine-related arrest in Taiwan against the general insured population, and as a cohort agreeing in direction with other designs; not for the size of an effect of methamphetamine, not for a dose–response, and not for an effect of rehabilitation.

key_findings.finding: Linked Taiwanese registries, 2007–2016: 74,601 adults arrested for illicit use of an amphetamine-type substance (every arrest urine-confirmed; index date = first arrest) and 298,404 insured adults with no record of illicit drug use, four per exposed person, frequency matched on index year, age and sex; people with a psychosis diagnosis recorded before the index date excluded from both groups.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Findings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The exposure covers 23 listed substances, including methamphetamine, amphetamine, dexamphetamine, MDMA, MDA, MDEA, brolamfetamine, DOM and lisdexamphetamine; no breakdown of the cohort by substance is given.

Both cohorts: mean age 33.3 (SD 9.45), 84.2% men. Comorbidities recorded during 2007–2016, amphetamine vs comparison cohort: depression 1.98% vs 0.42%, anxiety 0.91% vs 0.27%, ischaemic heart disease 1.32% vs 0.78%, cardiovascular disease 0.79% vs 0.45%, stroke 1.31% vs 0.66%. Mean follow-up 4.93 and 4.99 years (SD 2.93).
key_findings.locator: Findings, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: First recorded psychosis diagnosis: 1,722 in 367,696 person-years (4.68 per 1,000) vs 1,144 in 1,487,536 (0.77 per 1,000); crude HR 6.08 (95% CI 5.64–6.55); HR 5.28 (4.90–5.70) adjusted for age, sex and the five comorbidities.
key_findings.note: Rate difference about 3.9 per 1,000 person-years (editors' calculation). The abstract calls the adjusted HR 5.28 times more likely; the Findings use the same phrase for the crude ratio 6.08.

key_findings.finding: Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence of psychosis at the end of 10 years of follow-up: 3.75% in the amphetamine cohort vs 0.63% in the comparison cohort (log-rank p<0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Findings, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 (image; values not extracted beyond the text)
key_findings.note: Kaplan–Meier estimates with death treated as censoring (the number of deaths is not reported), so they describe the risk in the absence of death rather than observed proportions, and somewhat overstate the cumulative incidence when deaths compete (editors' note).

key_findings.finding: Adjusted HRs by age: 18–29 5.09 (4.50–5.75), 30–44 5.33 (4.79–5.93), 45 or older 5.41 (4.29–6.82). By sex: men 4.81 (4.42–5.24; rates 4.16 vs 0.77 per 1,000), women 7.49 (6.30–8.91; rates 7.33 vs 0.78). No interaction test is reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Age and Sex rows; Findings, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: By comorbidity: without comorbidity, rates 3.91 vs 0.62 per 1,000, adjusted HR 6.30 (5.79–6.86); with comorbidity, rates 20.02 vs 7.39 per 1,000, adjusted HR 2.28 (1.93–2.69). The authors read the larger HR without comorbidity as pointing to a direct effect of amphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Comorbidities rows; Findings, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: On the absolute scale the excess is larger with comorbidity: about 12.6 against 3.3 per 1,000 person-years (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: By number of arrests (counted from the index date to the end of the study), adjusted HRs against the comparison cohort: one 4.49 (4.09–4.93; 40,880 people, 4.40 per 1,000), two 5.07 (4.51–5.72), three 5.24 (4.52–6.09), four 5.53 (4.60–6.64), five or more 6.25 (5.42–7.20; 6,572 people, 5.45 per 1,000); p for trend 0.038, printed in the incidence-rate column. The authors state they could not assert dose dependence because the database has no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Findings, 4th paragraph; Methods › Statistics, 1st paragraph; Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Person-years per person rise from about 4.4 with one arrest to 6.5 with five or more (editors' calculation), so more arrests go with longer observation. A linear regression of the five category incidence rates on the number of arrests gives p = 0.038 (editors' calculation), which suggests that the printed trend test used the five rates rather than individual data.

key_findings.finding: Within the amphetamine cohort, the 7,733 people who received rehabilitation treatment during deferred prosecution had 112 psychosis diagnoses in 29,884 person-years (3.75 per 1,000) against 1,610 in 337,812 (4.77) among the 66,868 without; adjusted HR 0.74 (0.61–0.89), adjusted also for the number of arrests. Prosecutors offered deferred prosecution to about 10% of people arrested, those with promising treatment outcomes as judged by the prosecutors, and treatment took place in hospital psychiatric departments.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Findings, 4th paragraph; Conclusions and clinical implications, 5th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and that the results should be considered exploratory.

Limitations stated by the authors: amphetamine may precipitate rather than cause psychotic symptoms; arrests reflect police activity and priorities and do not capture all use (many people who use are never arrested), so the comparison group may include people who use and arrested people may use more often; severity of dependence is not documented; socio-economic status was not matched; prosecutors selected about 10% for rehabilitation; no genetic data or information on ethnic group, obstetric complications or childhood adversity; four controls per case may reduce representativeness; a single average HR may mislead; exposure could not be modelled as time-varying.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions and clinical implications, 6th to 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The comparison group's psychosis rate, 77 per 100,000 person-years, is described by the authors as slightly higher than published figures: pooled incidence of psychotic disorders 26.6 (international, 2002–17) and 31.7 per 100,000 person-years (England), and US rates of first psychotic symptoms of 86 (ages 15–29) and 46 per 100,000 (ages 30–59).
key_findings.note: 77 is 2.4 to 2.9 times the two pooled incidences of psychotic disorders (editors' arithmetic); slightly higher fits only the US symptom rates.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the psychosis definition includes other stimulant use disorders with psychosis, and the exclusion list for earlier psychosis contains the drug-induced psychosis codes 292.1, 292.11 and 292.12 (with 291.3, 291.5, 293.81, 293.82 and 297.3), but the list of outcome codes that ends follow-up does not contain them.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study population, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether substance-induced psychotic disorders were counted as outcomes. If they were not, the outcome is schizophrenia, affective disorders with psychotic features, other nonorganic psychoses and hallucinations, and the HR does not describe drug-induced psychosis; if they were, the printed code list is incomplete.

reporting_issues.issue: Comorbidities were assigned from diagnoses made at any time during 2007–2016 (Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph), yet Table 1 is titled as baseline factors; and the depression codes (296.20–296.24, 296.30–296.34) include 296.24 and 296.34, major depression with psychotic features, which are also outcome codes.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study population, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjustment for, and stratification by, comorbidity partly conditions on diagnoses made after exposure and on the outcome itself; the adjusted HR and the comorbidity strata (6.30 against 2.28) cannot be read as a conventional adjustment for baseline differences.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give the age groups as 18–35, 35–49 and 50 or older; Tables 1 and 2 use 18–29, 30–44 and 45 or older.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph; Tables 1–2
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables' groups are the ones analysed.

reporting_issues.issue: The p for trend (0.038) is printed in the incidence-rate column of Table 3 and the test is not described. A regression of the five category incidence rates (4.40, 4.80, 4.81, 4.84, 5.45) on the number of arrests reproduces p = 0.038 (editors' calculation, 3 degrees of freedom), while the adjusted HRs for one arrest and for five or more have non-overlapping intervals (4.09–4.93 and 5.42–7.20). Arrests were counted from the index date to the study end date, which implies that arrests after a psychosis diagnosis were also counted (this is not stated explicitly).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3; Methods › Statistics, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The trend test appears to treat five group rates as five observations; the gradient should be cited without this p value, and in any case as a gradient in arrests counted over the whole follow-up, not in amount of use.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions call the rates of 77 and 468 per 100,000 persons annual cumulative incidence rates; they are the incidence rates per person-year of Table 2 (0.77 and 4.68 per 1,000 person-years). The comparison group's 77 is called slightly higher than published incidences of 26.6 and 31.7 per 100,000 person-years for psychotic disorders.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Conclusions and clinical implications, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: A rate 2.4 to 2.9 times the cited incidence of psychotic disorders (editors' arithmetic) shows that the outcome is broader than psychotic disorder as usually counted; slightly higher understates the gap.

reporting_issues.issue: The same phrase, times more likely, is used for the crude rate ratio (6.08, Findings, 2nd paragraph) and for the adjusted HR (5.28, abstract).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Findings; Findings, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the headline figure is an adjusted hazard ratio, not a ratio of risks.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10231478 (all sections; Tables 1–4 rendered as text with footnotes; funding, competing-interest, contributor and data statements; Figure 1, the selection flowchart, and Figure 2, the Kaplan–Meier curves, are images and their values were not extracted beyond the text; the article has no supplement)

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 22: corrected: the finding should say that arrests reflect police activity and priorities and do not capture all use, since many people who use are never arrested, rather than that they miss most use; 'most' is not the authors' word. The rest of the list matches the Conclusions, 6th to 10th paragraphs.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Conclusions and clinical implications, 6th paragraph (arrest reflects police activity and priorities; it does not capture all use; many people who use will never be detected or arrested). Corrected as the reader proposes.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 22: missed (minor): the Cox models and the Kaplan–Meier curves treat death as censoring, and the number of deaths is not reported; the 10-year cumulative incidences (3.75% vs 0.63%) are therefore Kaplan–Meier estimates for a world without death and overstate the actual cumulative incidence somewhat; claims citing them could say 'Kaplan–Meier estimate'.
